One thing that stands out to me about September 10 in the days and weeks preceding the 11th is This was a period that environmentalists had been waiting for and advocating for where the attention of the Congress and the country could be finally placed on this emerging crisis. And of course, all of that changed the following day. It was a very different place in the months leading up to September 11th, a very different set of national priorities, very different mood in the country, a different sense of our own security. You know, as always, very secure in our homeland. And the last thing any of us could imagine would be a major attack on American soil. We've been the subject of different terrorist attacks and plots in the past, but nothing like we would experience. And it would propel the country in a very different direction.
So on the morning of September 11th, where were you? And where were you first heard that plain had struck the World Trade Center?

At that point, I was renting an apartment a few blocks away from the Capitol. And I was preparing to walk to the Capitol when the first plane struck. And I couldn't figure out what I was seeing. I didn't understand what I was seeing. You know, could a plane bring down a whole building? And so I was still processing what was going on when I left my apartment to go to the Capitol to find out And what was happening, what our response was going to be when one of the aircraft hit the Pentagon. And I heard a boom, which I later learned was a secondary explosion, I think, when the fuel exploded. And there were people streaming through the streets away from the Capitol. I was trying to get to the Capitol to find out where was Congress going to convene. I wanted to make sure that my staff were OK and out of the building. We didn't know that there was still another aircraft that was on its way to the Capitol. And it was just chaos. And I remember stopping a policeman and asking, where is the Congress going to convene? And being told that we were going to meet at the police department, which turned out not to be true. And then trying to get through to my wife on my phone to let her know I was OK. We finally did connect as I was understanding in the street and let her know where I was and what was going on and that I was okay and just remember the anxiety and her voice. The next, I think, couple hours was spent trying to figure out where are we going to convene. And then one of the more memorable parts of that day was

And one of the things that I concluded was that a lot of what Al Qaeda was doing was designed to provoke a reaction. to provoke a commitment of resources by the United States that were unsustainable. And in fact, in that respect, we devoted enormous amounts of our most precious resource, the deployment of our troops, the risk of the lives of our troops, but also untold trillions of dollars in this effort to fight what attacked us on 9-11. Some of that response was probably what Al Qaeda was hoping for. So I think that it took us a very long time to realize that what we were doing was effective in part, but ineffective in other part.
